title: Why AI Isn’t Ready to Tackle Our Convoluted Genomes
gist: Philip Ball (via Quanta) argues the human genome is a dynamic, context-dependent regulatory system rather than a blueprint or program, driven by combinatorial transcription factors, distal enhancers, 3D chromatin folding, epigenetics, microRNAs and splicing. As a result, sequence-trained genomic foundation models like AlphaGenome, Evo 2 and Genos will likely be useful but limited, since key information lies in cell context and extra-genetic factors.

themes.theme: Limits of genomic AI foundation models

insights.claim: Genomic foundation models such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome are trained on vast genomic data to predict how DNA sequence differences affect biological processes and traits, including disease risk, while leaving regulatory complexity implicit in their training.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Identifies the main AI-for-genomics model landscape investors are betting on.
insights.quote: Genomic “foundation models” such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome are trained on vast quantities of genomic data
insights.locator: Some are counting on outsourcing the analysis

insights.claim: Author Philip Ball argues sequence-only genomic AI is likely useful but may fundamentally fall short, because the genome may not obey the straightforward input-output mapping such models assume.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Caps expectations for sequence-to-trait prediction products in drug discovery and diagnostics.
insights.quote: the genome might not submit to the kind of straightforward input-output approach that such AI models ultimately assume
insights.locator: This approach is likely to be useful

insights.claim: Because the genome behaves as an open, context-dependent informational system rather than a deterministic program, AI that relies solely on genetic sequences to predict genome behavior faces a structural challenge.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Suggests winning genomic-AI approaches will need multimodal, cell-context data, not just sequence.
insights.quote: This poses a challenge if AI relies solely on the genetic sequences within genomes to predict what genomes will do.

insights.claim: University of Edinburgh genome biologist Wendy Bickmore expects AlphaGenome to be useful but limited, citing missing data on the body's many cell types and how they change over development as the big gap.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Points to cell-type and developmental datasets as the bottleneck and potential value pool in genomic AI.
insights.quote: I’m sure [AlphaGenome] is going to be useful, but with limitations

insights.claim: Adrian Woolfson, cofounder of generative-biology company Genyro, argues genomic foundation models cannot predict all consequences of mutations because relevant information sits outside the genome sequence, in a broader 'informiome' including diet, environment, microbiome and culture.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Even an AI-biology founder flags hard limits on sequence-only models, relevant to valuing such startups.

insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Frames AI in biology as an augmenting tool rather than a replacement for mechanistic science.

themes.theme: Gene regulation complexity beyond the DNA code

insights.claim: Barely 2 percent of the roughly 3-billion-letter human genome consists of actual protein-coding genes (around 20,000 of them), so knowing the full sequence from the Human Genome Project has not explained how the genome works.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Shows why sequencing alone has not delivered the expected biological payoff.
insights.quote: barely 2 percent of the human genome consists of actual genes

insights.claim: In bacteria gene regulation follows largely 'OR' logic with single on/off signals, whereas in humans it resembles 'AND' logic integrating many signals, making regulatory knobs tunable and context-sensitive.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Combinatorial regulation is why simple target-to-trait models struggle in human biology.

insights.claim: The human genome has hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of enhancers, far more than genes, with many-to-many mappings between enhancers and genes, and their locations and targets are still largely unknown.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Large unmapped regulatory territory represents both a data gap and an opportunity for genomics tools.
insights.quote: It’s embarrassing that 25 years after the Human Genome Project, we don’t know where all the enhancers are in the genome
insights.locator: Enhancers are gathering points for transcription factors

insights.claim: Gene transcription depends on the 3D shape of chromatin, including cohesin-formed loops, topologically associating domains, and fluid transcription hubs that differ between even notionally identical cells.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Implies genome function requires spatial and single-cell data, not just linear sequence.
insights.quote: We’ve stopped thinking about the genome as a linear piece of DNA code

insights.claim: Additional regulatory layers after transcription, such as microRNAs silencing mRNAs and context-sensitive splicing by the spliceosome producing different protein isoforms, further decouple DNA sequence from protein outcome.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Multiple regulatory checkpoints increase uncertainty in predicting drug targets from sequence.

insights.claim: Some researchers speak of an 'epigenetic code', but it is far from clear that any such systematic code for epigenetic marks really exists.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Cautions against assuming epigenetics is a cleanly decodable layer for AI or therapeutics.

themes.theme: Why the genome evolved this complexity

insights.claim: Bickmore suspects regulatory and genome-organization complexity may have been the only way to generate organismal complexity: more tissue types demanded more enhancers, placed ever farther from genes, which in turn required TADs and 3D folding.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Explains why complex-organism biology resists the simpler models that worked in bacteria.
insights.quote: As you get more complexity, you need to add more and more enhancers

insights.claim: Transposable elements accumulated from parasitic viruses forced the evolution of extra regulatory layers to keep cells from translating unneeded or harmful RNAs.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Adds another context-dependent layer that sequence models must capture.

insights.claim: The genome acts as a recursive, self-referential 'strange loop' in Douglas Hofstadter's sense, since its regulators are themselves produced by the same context-dependent genomic process, so it is not a blueprint.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Reframes genomics as a dynamic-systems problem, shaping which AI architectures and data might work.

insights.claim: No human technology works the way the genome does, so metaphors like blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short; Barbara McClintock's view of the genome as a sensitive, responsive organ is closer to the truth.
insights.speaker: Philip Ball
insights.so_what: Signals the field's conceptual shift away from code-centric models that underpin many genomics investment theses.
insights.quote: There is no human technology that works this way, so metaphors such as blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short.
